claim.pdf_says: '8.5.1.4   Limitations of character handling' and '8.5.1.5   Algebraic signs' are printed as fourth-level clause headings, subordinate to '8.5.1  Computer independent data description', in the same typographic rank as their siblings 8.5.1.1 General, 8.5.1.2 Files and records and 8.5.1.3 Levels.
claim.markdown_says: specs/ISO_COBOL.md line 7977 '## 8.5.1.4 Limitations of character handling' and line 7996 '## 8.5.1.5 Algebraic signs' - level 2 - while their parent is line 7901 '### 8.5.1 Computer independent data description' (level 3) and their siblings are line 7904 '#### 8.5.1.1 General', 7911 '#### 8.5.1.2 Files and records', 7922 '#### 8.5.1.3 Levels' (level 4). The children are therefore one level SHALLOWER than the clause that contains them, i.e. the outline is inverted, and they sit at the same level as the '## Page N' scaffolding heading.
claim.why_it_matters: Any table of contents, outline view, or anchor-based navigation generated from the markdown misrepresents the standard's clause hierarchy - subclauses detach from their parent clause and appear as peers of clause 8.5 or of the page furniture. For a spec used as the citation authority, a reader following the outline can attribute a rule to the wrong clause. The same inversion recurs across this batch and beyond, so it is a mechanical transcription defect, not a local slip.

verdict.reasoning: REFUTED. Rendered PDF page 183 (printed 153) at 300 dpi and compared it glyph-for-glyph against E:/Temp/specrecon/v183/page-183.md and specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 7976-8010. (1) NOTHING IS MISSING. The kind label 'missing-heading' is false on its face: both headings are present in the markdown with verbatim-identical text and verbatim-identical clause numbers - '8.5.1.4 Limitations of character handling' (line 7977) and '8.5.1.5 Algebraic signs' (line 7996). So is every word of the page body: the lead paragraph, enumerated items 1) and 2), the NOTE, both em-dash sub-bullets, the 'These techniques facilitate...' and 'COBOL does not provide any special handling...' paragraphs, and all three paragraphs of 8.5.1.5. The only text-level differences are the multi-space tab between clause number and title collapsing to one space, and the PDF's line-break hyphen in 'reference-/modification' being correctly rejoined - pure whitespace and hyphenation. (2) THE CLAIM ATTRIBUTES A TYPOGRAPHIC HIERARCHY TO THE PDF THAT THE PRINTED PAGE DOES NOT CONTAIN. I rendered page 181 (printed 151) to inspect the siblings the claim invokes. On that page '8.5 Data description and representation', '8.5.1 Computer independent data description', '8.5.1.1 General', '8.5.1.2 Files and records', '8.5.1.3 Levels' and '8.5.1.3.1 General' are all set in the SAME bold serif face, at the SAME point size, flush at the SAME left margin, with no indentation, size, weight, numbering-style or leading difference between a second-level clause and a fifth-level one. Page 183's '8.5.1.4' and '8.5.1.5' are set identically to all of them. ISO conveys depth here exclusively through the dotted clause number, which the markdown reproduces exactly. There is therefore NO printed depth signal for the transcription to have lost, and the claim's premise that the PDF ranks 8.5.1.4 below 8.5.1 but level with 8.5.1.1-.3 is not what the page shows - the PDF ranks all of them identically. (3) WHAT REMAINS IS MARKDOWN ATX DEPTH, WHICH IS FORMATTING AND CHANGES NO MEANING. '##' versus '####' is a transcription-internal convention, not a transcription of a printed feature, and the clause number in the heading text makes the hierarchy fully explicit and machine-recoverable regardless of hash count. (4) THE 'WHY IT MATTERS' RATIONALE IS ALREADY FALSE DOCUMENT-WIDE BY CONSTRUCTION, INDEPENDENT OF THESE TWO HEADINGS. The transcription emits the running header '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' as a LEVEL-1 heading 941 times and '## Page N' as a LEVEL-2 heading 1261 times. A level-1 heading recurring on nearly every page resets any depth-derived outline continuously, so no meaningful outline can be built from ATX depth anywhere in this file - the alleged harm does not originate at 8.5.1.4. Navigation in this transcription runs on the explicit TOC plus anchors, and both are present and CORRECT for these clauses: line 289 '[8.5.1.4 Limitations of character handling](#section-8-5-1-4) ... [153](#page-153)' and line 290 for 8.5.1.5 resolve to the anchors '' (line 7976) and '' (line 7995), immediately above the right headings, on the right printed page. A reader following the actual navigation mechanism lands on the correct clause, and a citer reads the clause number off the heading text. No rule can be attributed to the wrong clause. Zero content differs between the PDF and the markdown on page 183.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a PDF-vs-markdown content discrepancy. Page 183 transcribes completely and faithfully: both clause headings and all body text, notes and bullets are present verbatim, and the TOC entries (lines 289-290) and anchors (lines 7976, 7995) point correctly at them. The residual observation - that ISO_COBOL.md's ATX depths are internally inconsistent within clause 8.5.1 (8.5.1.1-.3 and 8.5.1.3.1 use '####', while 8.5.1.3.2, 8.5.1.3.3, 8.5.1.4, 8.5.1.5 and 8.5.1.6 use '##') - is a cosmetic inconsistency in the transcription's own markup convention, not a loss of anything the PDF prints, since the PDF sets clause headings from 8.5 through 8.5.1.3.1 in one identical bold face at one identical size and margin and encodes depth only in the dotted clause number, which the markdown preserves exactly. Heading depth is not the file's navigation mechanism in any case: '# ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' appears as a level-1 heading 941 times and '## Page N' as level-2 1261 times, so depth-derived outlines are already meaningless throughout by design. If the owner wants uniform hash depths for tooling reasons, that is a global markup-normalization chore across the whole file, not a page-183 spec-fidelity defect, and it should not be logged as 'missing-heading' since no heading is missing.
